title: Strength to the weary
hookLine: a later blessing thanks God for giving strength to the tired
tomorrow: The soul you gave me is pure

cards: Not everybody wakes up rested. The baby was up at three. The worry was up at four.
Some mornings the first thing you feel is how heavy your arms are. A prayer book that only thanked God for bright, bouncing mornings would leave a lot of people out.
So near the end of the morning blessings, many prayer books carry one that seems written for exactly this person. It isn't in the Talmud's list. It came later, and it stuck.

teach.b: The words are: blessed are you, hanoten laya'ef koach, who gives strength to the weary.
The phrase comes from Isaiah, chapter forty, in the old Jewish translation: "He giveth power to the faint."

A few verses on, Isaiah promises that those who wait for God will renew their strength, and run, and not be weary. Ya'ef means worn out from effort, the tiredness of someone who has been working or walking a long way.
The Talmud's list of waking blessings doesn't include this one. It shows up in the medieval prayer books of France and Germany, and spread from there.
Some authorities hesitated: Rabbi Joseph Karo, author of the Shulchan Aruch, the code of Jewish law, was uneasy about a blessing the Talmud never mentions.
But the custom held, and today it's widely said, in many communities as the last of the morning blessings. Look where it lands.
After the blessings for eyes and legs and clothes, one more line admits something honest: you're up, but you may not be full of energy. It doesn't say who makes the weary cheerful.
It says who gives them strength, enough to begin.
Sleep is treated as a gift that restores, and the morning thanks God for what was restored, even if only partly.

how: Many Jewish prayer books include the blessing 'who gives strength to the weary' among the morning blessings, often as the last of the series, said at home or at the start of the morning service.

sad, weighed down by grief or by worry
lazy, unwilling to get up and do the work

games.q: you're a medieval rabbi. a popular morning blessing isn't in the Talmud. people love it. what do you do?
o: hesitate, but the people keep saying it.
games.why: some authorities, including Joseph Karo, were uneasy. the custom held, and many prayer books carry it today.

practice: Let your shoulders drop and your hands go heavy, and admit how tired you actually are right now, on a scale of one to ten.
Then breathe slowly and feel what's still there under the tiredness: a heartbeat, a breath, enough strength to sit here. If you pray, you can say hanoten laya'ef koach.

wordCard.voice: Ya'ef. Worn out from effort — the later morning blessing hanoten laya'ef koach gives strength to everyone who wakes up tired, even partly restored.

orig.note: Hebrew: who gives strength to the weary, from Isaiah 40:29.

carryVoice: Your line: enough to begin. Not cheerful, not full of energy, just strong enough to start. That's day five hundred forty-five.
